Project Brief version 2

Download the PDF The same Brief as a two-page document.

1. The organization

Fernhill Software is a useful fiction, a business-software firm with about 1,100 engineers in 120 product teams. It hires engineers on technical skill and promotes its strongest into management, where some struggle. In 2025, as AI coding tools arrive, an AI enthusiast on the leadership team proposes a three-part reorganization. First, hire professional managers on people skill instead of promoting engineers. Second, make each team’s engineer-manager its technical lead, keeping technical judgment but managing no one. Third, let AI fill the manager’s technical gaps. Fernhill runs a one-year pilot from July 2025, assigning its 120 teams by lot to three arms of 40 so the reorganization and AI can be told apart.

2. The model

A team delivers when two jobs get done, coordinating people and resolving technical unknowns. The proposal splits those jobs between a manager and a lead, with AI assisting both.

  1. People skill lowers coordination friction. Less work sits blocked on other people, more so in bigger teams.
  2. Difficulty sets how many unknowns arrive. AI resolves routine ones but helps little on hard ones.
  3. Escalated unknowns queue at whoever holds technical judgment, the engineer-manager or a tech lead with far more time. Near capacity, the wait explodes (Little’s Law).

In short, AI should help most on easy work, and the new structure most on hard work, where queues form.

For the model to be right, the professional managers must have more people skill than the engineer-managers they replace. Teams must stay in their arm, and teams without AI must go without it. The leads must accept their new role. Difficulty must be judgeable at quarterly planning. What stays unmeasured is the judgment holder’s capacity, which shows only through waits.

3. The question

Should Fernhill replace engineer-managers with professional managers backed by technical leads and AI? The pilot answers with two comparisons, with each arm also set against its own eight pre-pilot quarters. The first compares AI, holding structure fixed (engineer-managers with and without AI). The second compares structure, holding AI fixed (manager + lead vs. engineer-manager, both with AI), the decision Fernhill faces.

4. The prediction

Stated before looking at this version’s data:

  • AI alone raises delivery on easy quarters by about 8 points, and cuts their escalations by about 40%, but changes little on hard quarters.
  • People-skill ratings are higher under professional managers.
  • The new structure shortens escalation waits, most on hard quarters, and on hard quarters delivers about 5 points more than engineer-managers with AI.

The model is wrong if any of these holds:

  • AI’s gain is as large on hard quarters as on easy ones.
  • The new structure’s waits are no shorter on hard quarters.
  • Its waits are shorter but its delivery is no better. Then the queue isn’t what limits delivery.

5. The data sketch

The data. Fernhill’s records have one row per team per quarter, July 2023 to June 2026 (1,440 rows), and they are simulated, since Fernhill is fictional. The variables, by concept. The change is arm (assigned by lot), manager type, and AI licenses, with IT’s usage logs. The manager has a people-skill rating on the eight Project Oxygen behaviors, and the hours work sits blocked on other teams. The work has team size, and difficulty rated at planning (a rating new with the pilot). Unknowns are escalations, and the hours each waits. The outcome is the share of committed milestones delivered on time.

6. The disciplinary anchor

Whom to promote (organizational management). Firms promote their best performers, who then make worse managers (Peter and Hull, 1969; Benson, Li and Shue, 2019). People skill keeps teams together, and Google’s Project Oxygen ranked technical skill last of eight manager behaviors (Hoffman and Tadelis, 2021; Garvin, 2013).

The work itself (operations management). Unknowns go up the hierarchy unless knowledge is cheap, and AI makes only routine knowledge cheap (Galbraith, 1974; Garicano, 2000; Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, 2025; METR, 2025). Waits grow when escalations arrive faster than they are cleared (Little’s Law).

The method. The pilot is randomized, so the lot makes the arms comparable and their differences are the effects of AI and of the structure.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) to turn the critique of version 1 into a pilot design and size its arms. It suggested a fourth arm, a professional manager without AI. I rejected it, since three arms answer the decision Fernhill faces. It suggested surveying how managers and leads work together. I left that out, since the escalation wait already measures how fast technical questions get answered.

Data & Methods draft version 2

Download the PDF The same draft as a two-page document, with its charts.

1. Unit of observation

One row of my data is one product team in one quarter, because the lot assigns whole teams and delivery is counted by the quarter. There are 1,440 rows, from 120 teams over 12 quarters, July 2023 to June 2026, eight before the pilot and four during it. The lot assigned teams, 40 to each of three arms (engineer-managers without AI, engineer-managers with AI, and a manager and lead with AI), so arm comparisons rest on 40 teams each, not on 480 team-quarters.

2. Variable table

Concept Variable Kind Source What it misses
Structure and AI arm Labels Pilot register Drift from the arm
Before or after period Labels Calendar Half-done quarters
Unknowns escalations Counts Tracker Hallway answers
Waiting esc_wait_hrs Measurement (hours) Tracker Untracked waits
Difficulty hard_plan Yes/No Planning review Misjudged quarters
Delivery delivered_share Measurement (share) Planning tool Customer value and renegotiation

3. Data source

Fernhill’s pilot register, issue tracker, planning review, and planning tool, read through People Analytics, cover all 120 teams for all 12 quarters. The planning review has rated difficulty only since July 2025. A second file from IT logs AI use by team for the four pilot quarters. The main file also holds records my model doesn’t call for (departures, the lead’s former role). Gemini suggested describing them, and I left them out. I use escalations still open at quarter’s close, and the usage logs, only as checks on the queue and on the no-AI arm. Fernhill is a useful fiction, so these records are simulated, but not from the model above. They come from a model this version doesn’t see, whose units are these team-quarters and whose relationships, noise, and assumptions are published in Module 3. Until then, I treat them as the firm’s records.

4. Quality concern

The difficulty rating at planning is the most likely to mislead. It is mismeasured whenever planners misjudge a quarter, and missing before July 2025, when nobody rated difficulty at planning. If planners misjudge, I would see quarters rated easy with as many escalations as hard ones, which makes the hard–easy difference look smaller. I will split results by the planning rating, never by the close-of-quarter rating made after the outcome, and say that misjudged quarters shrink any difference. The before-period has no rating, so it enters only unsplit, as each arm’s baseline.

5. First description

Delivery (delivered_share). Kind: a measurement, a share from 0 to 1. How many: 1,440, none blank. Middle: median 0.68, and mean 0.64, which a tail of bad quarters pulls down. Spread: half fall between 0.50 and 0.82, and the range is 0 to 1. Shape: skewed left, with a long tail of quarters that delivered little (24 under 5%). Choice: each team-quarter counts once, whatever its size. Weighting by milestones gives 0.63.

Against my model: not yet able to say, since one variable can’t show whether the arms differ.

Waiting (esc_wait_hrs). Kind: a measurement, in hours. How many: 1,399, with 41 blank (3%). The gaps are in the tracker, before and during the pilot. Middle: median 15.5 hours, and mean 28.6, which a few very long waits pull up. Spread: half fall between 8.4 and 34.7 hours, and the range is 3.2 to 1,382. Shape: skewed far right, with 30 team-quarters waiting over 100 hours, the longest about eight weeks. Choice: blanks left out. Long waits kept, since nothing says they are errors, and the chart stops at 100 hours.

Against my model: not yet able to say. A long right tail is what any queue produces, and one variable can’t show whether the structure changes it. Whose waits they are is a comparison for Module 2.

Difficulty (hard_plan). Kind: Yes/No. How many: 480, all in the pilot, with 960 blank before July 2025, when the rating didn’t exist. Middle, spread and shape: 0.44 rated hard (210 quarters). With two values, the proportion says it all. Against my model: not yet able to say, but there are enough quarters of each kind to compare the arms on hard and easy work.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) for the counts, middles, spreads, and histograms. I kept the median for waits, since long waits pull the mean, and rejected its offer to drop waits over 100 hours, since nothing says they are errors.

Work it yourself: the Data & Methods prompts version 2

These are the prompts used to write the Data & Methods draft above, in order. Download fernhill_v2.csv, start a new Gemini chat with your Willamette account, upload the file, and paste each prompt into the same chat. (The Results prompts that follow continue in the same chat.) Think about the question before you open “What we found.” Gemini’s wording and charts will differ from ours, but the numbers should match. If a number doesn’t, that’s a check worth running.

A rerun on Gemini 4. We ran every prompt again on November 16 with Gemini’s newer model (the shared chat is https://gemini.google.com/share/d/1L3ukbrI0Up9kUio2GSfEAZk94D-X2nU0?usp=sharing). Every number came out as it does here, and the notes that begin “In a rerun” say what was different. Part way through, Gemini said the file was no longer attached. If yours does, attach it again and repeat the prompt.

What is new since version 1. The file now has three arms and a before-period, so a row’s group matters. Two of the three variables are new to the model (the wait, and difficulty rated at planning). And this time the prompts tell Gemini what a column means before it can guess, which is the lesson of version 1’s hard_close and people_rating.

See exactly how we ran it Gemini's answers to these prompts, step by step (the shared chat, which opens when you sign in with your Willamette account).

P1

What is a row, and what is compared?

What does one row of my data represent? How many rows are there, how many different teams do they cover, how many quarters, and how many teams are in each arm? Which quarters come before the pilot and which during it?

The lot assigned teams, not team-quarters. How many units does each arm really have?

What we found

One row is one product team in one quarter, and there are 1,440 rows, 120 teams, 12 quarters (2023Q3 to 2026Q2), eight before the pilot (2023Q3 to 2025Q2, 960 rows) and four during it (2025Q3 to 2026Q2, 480 rows). Each of the three arms has 40 teams, and each team stays in its arm in all 12 quarters, so an arm comparison rests on 40 teams an arm, not on 480 team-quarters.

Gemini may also check, unprompted, that no team appears twice in a quarter (none does). Its listing of the columns shows where the blanks are. hard_plan is blank for all 960 rows before the pilot, esc_wait_hrs has 41 blanks, and lead_former_manager is blank in all but 160 rows (the manager-and-lead arm during the pilot, the only place there is a lead with a former role). Check the AI’s count against something you know. Here, 120 teams times 12 quarters is 1,440, and 3 arms times 40 teams is 120. In our run Gemini gave all of these correctly, but it did not say that the team is the unit the lot assigned, and it did not mention the blanks, so the unit and the blanks are yours to add.

P2

Describe the outcome

Describe delivered_share: what kind of variable it is, how many values there are including blanks, the middle (the median, and the mean only if a mean makes sense for this kind of variable), how spread out it is, and its shape, with a histogram in five-point bands. Tell me any choices you made, such as dropping blanks or zeros, and whether each team-quarter counts once or is weighted.

Which is larger, the mean or the median? Why?

What we found
Question Answer
Kind A measurement, a share from 0 to 1
How many 1,440, none blank
Middle Median 0.68, and mean 0.64
Spread Half fall between 0.50 and 0.82, and the range is 0 to 1
Shape Skewed left, with a long tail of quarters that delivered little (24 are under 5%)

The mean sits below the median because of that tail. A choice worth naming. Each team-quarter counts once, whatever its size. Weighting by milestones (all milestones delivered divided by all committed) gives 0.63. Gemini will list its own choices (here, nothing dropped, 20 zeros kept, no rescaling) and may add that 39 quarters delivered everything. Read its list against the one above, and ask it to show the code for any count you want to trust. In our run it kept every value, said each team-quarter counts once, and listed the zeros (20) and the perfect quarters (39) correctly, but it did not offer the milestone-weighted figure, so that choice was ours to name. Version 1’s file gave 0.69 and 0.65, so small differences between the two files are expected.

P3

Describe a measurement with a long tail

Describe esc_wait_hrs the same way. Tell me how many are blank and in which periods, and show a histogram in five-hour bands that stops at 100 hours. Tell me how many waits the chart leaves off and how long the longest is, and what you did with the long waits.

A few waits are very long. Are they errors? What would you need to know to decide, and which summary would you use for the middle?

What we found
Question Answer
Kind A measurement, in hours
How many 1,399, with 41 blank (3%), 32 before the pilot and 9 during it
Middle Median 15.5 hours, and mean 28.6
Spread Half fall between 8.4 and 34.7 hours, and the range is 3.2 to 1,382.2
Shape Skewed far right, with 30 waits over 100 hours (the longest is about eight weeks)

The mean is nearly twice the median because of a few very long waits, so the median is the honest middle. Gemini may offer to drop the waits over 100 hours as outliers, or to put the axis on a log scale. In our run it did neither. It kept every wait in the statistics, capped only the chart at 100 hours, reported the 30 it left off and the longest (1,382.2 hours), and called the long ones “extreme outliers,” a label to question, since it says they are unusual, not wrong. It also described the column as an average wait per escalation, a reading from the name. A log axis is a way to draw them, not a reason to remove them. Nothing says they are errors, so the draft keeps them, says so, and lets the chart stop at 100 hours with its caption reporting the 30 it leaves off. Whose waits they are is a comparison for the Results draft. The blanks are 3% of the column and spread across all three arms (15, 11 and 15 rows), so the draft leaves them out and says so.

P4

Describe a yes/no variable, and tell the AI what it means

Describe hard_plan the same way. In this file it is "yes" when the quarterly planning review, held before the work starts, rated the quarter as hard for the team, and the review has only rated difficulty since July 2025. Tell me how many values are blank and which rows they are.

What did this prompt tell Gemini that version 1's hard_close prompt left for a correction?

What we found

Yes/No, 480 values, all in the pilot. 210 quarters were rated hard (0.44), and 270 were not. The other 960 rows, every quarter before July 2025, are blank, because nobody rated difficulty at planning then. Those blanks are by design, not mistakes. With two values the proportion says it all, and Gemini may call 0.44 a “binary mean,” which is the same number, a share. The mix is similar in all three arms (41%, 44% and 46% hard), so no arm drew a much easier year by luck.

In our run Gemini gave the counts correctly, listed the blank rows (the first 960), and showed the share rated hard by quarter (38% to 48%), though not by arm. Because you told it what the column means, Gemini has no reason to guess. Compare that with version 1, where hard_close was a name and Gemini made up a meaning. The meaning came from the dictionary, not the file, and it is worth pasting in whenever a column’s name can be read two ways.

P5

Where could it mislead you?

My data is Fernhill Software's records, one row per product team per quarter. For each of these, say whether it could affect my data and what I would see in the data if it were happening: missing values, mismeasurement, a definition that changed, only some cases recorded, dates or entries shifted. Focus on hard_plan.

Which way is most likely to mislead you about difficulty? What would you see if it were happening?

What we found

In our run Gemini said yes to all five and ranked none. Choosing is your work. For mismeasurement it already pointed to the disagreement with hard_close (43 quarters planned easy and closed hard), which is the check the next prompt runs properly. Two of them are true of hard_plan in different senses. It is missing for 960 rows by design, so no comparison of the pilot with the before-period can be split by difficulty. And it is mismeasured whenever planners misjudge a quarter, since the rating is a prediction made before the work. A planner who misjudged would produce quarters rated easy that had as many escalations as hard ones, and that would shrink any difference between hard and easy quarters. The draft picks the rating, says it will split by it and never by the close-of-quarter rating, and says misjudged quarters make any hard–easy difference look smaller than it is. What you owe the reader is one choice, what you would see if it were happening, and what you will do.

In the pilot quarters, compare the average escalations and the average delivered_share for hard_plan = yes and hard_plan = no, and tell me how many quarters rated easy had 10 or more escalations. Then cross-tabulate hard_plan with hard_close and tell me how often they agree.

If planners misjudged difficulty a lot, what would you see in the escalations? Which of the two ratings would you rather split by, and why?

What we found
Pilot quarters Rated hard at planning Rated easy at planning
Quarters 210 270
Average escalations 12.4 4.9
Average delivered_share 49.2% 71.6%
With 10 or more escalations 140 (67%) 28 (10%)
Closed as hard Closed as not hard
Planned hard 164 46
Planned easy 43 227

The planning rating is informative, though not perfect. Hard quarters have about two and a half times the escalations, and only one easy quarter in ten had 10 or more. The two ratings agree on 391 of 480 quarters (81%). Gemini’s own answer matched every number above (it also wrote “significantly” with no test behind it, a word to question). It did not split delivery by the close rating. Ask it to, and delivery is 43.6% against 75.6% (a gap of 32 points), against 49.2% and 71.6% (22 points) by the planning rating. The close rating separates delivery more, as you would expect if part of it is the outcome leaking in. That is the reason to split by hard_plan, and the reason the draft says misjudged quarters make its differences conservative.

P6

Hold it up against the prediction

My model predicts that AI helps most on easy quarters, that the new structure shortens escalation waits, and that on hard quarters the new structure delivers about 5 points more than engineer-managers with AI. Based only on the descriptions above, does the data look the way the model says it should? What can a description of one variable at a time not tell me?

What would you write for each of the three predictions, using only what you have described so far?

What we found

From the descriptions alone, not yet able to say, for all three. Each description is of one variable at a time, and none can show how the arms differ, whether the wait is shorter in one of them, or whether anything is higher on hard quarters. “Not yet able to say” is an honest sentence, and a better one than a confident sentence you can’t back.

Gemini did not stop there. Asked to use “only the descriptions above,” it went back to the file and compared the arms itself, which is the Results draft arriving early. In our run its numbers were right, and its verdicts were worth reading closely.

  • AI helps most on easy quarters: “partially supported.” It gave the raw gaps, +10.7 points on easy quarters and +9.5 on hard, and called the easy gap slightly larger. It did not use the before-period yet, and the Brief’s first “model is wrong if” line asks whether the hard gap is as large as the easy one.
  • The new structure shortens waits: “contradicted.” It used the average wait over all pilot quarters, 53.2 hours for the new structure against 22.4 for engineer-managers with AI (medians 15.0 against 11.5), with no split by difficulty. Those numbers are right, and they answer a different question from the Brief’s, which is about hard quarters. A later prompt shows the median on hard quarters pointing the other way.
  • The new structure delivers more on hard quarters: “contradicted.” It gave 46.3% against 55.3%, about 8.9 points lower, which is right.

It used hard_plan, not hard_close, and it did not say “significant.” Three things to read closely:

  • Counts against units. A comparison across 160 team-quarters an arm in the pilot is a comparison of 40 teams an arm.
  • Which summary and which quarters. Its wait verdict used the average, over all quarters. Ask what the median says, and what it says on hard quarters.
  • A verdict is not a result. “Contradicted” arrived before the before-period, the median or the difficulty split. Hold your own verdict until the Results prompts are done.

Its second answer is the useful one. A single variable can’t show a difference between arms, a change from the before-period, how a wait relates to delivery, or whether a few extreme values belong to one arm. That is exactly what the Results prompts are for.

In a rerun on Gemini 4 (November 16) Gemini did not go back to the file. It said it could not tell for any of the three predictions, listed what each would need (the arms split out, the waits by arm and period, the hard quarters by arm), and named the difference in differences in passing as something a one-variable description cannot show. That is the answer this prompt is looking for. If yours does compare the arms, read its verdicts as the Results draft arriving early.

Results draft version 2

Download the PDF The same draft as a two-page document, with its charts.

1. The question and the prediction

My question is causal. With AI held fixed, does the new structure raise delivery (the share of a team’s committed milestones delivered by their dates) above engineer-managers’, and what does AI alone add? The lot would let me call differences effects, but this draft only describes them and leaves the causal claim for Module 3. My model predicts AI adds about 8 points on easy quarters and cuts their escalations about 40%, higher ratings under professional managers, and that the new structure shortens waits and adds about 5 points on hard quarters.

2. The charts

This chart answers: how does delivery compare across the three arms on easy and hard quarters?

Delivery is a measurement (a share), the arm is a label, and difficulty at planning is yes/no. Each dot is one arm’s average over its pilot team-quarters of that kind (66 to 94), and each cross is its average over the eight quarters before the pilot (320).

This chart answers: where do each arm’s hard quarters end up on delivery, with and without the first pilot quarter (a honeymoon check), and which had a wait over 100 hours (solid)? Arms are labels, the wait is hours, delivery is a share, and a ribbon is a count of team-quarters. Boxes give an arm’s count in a band, long waits in brackets.

3. The association

On AI alone, engineer-managers with AI delivered 10.7 points more on easy quarters and 9.5 more on hard ones than those without. Each comparison has 320 pilot team-quarters from 80 teams offered AI. But the lot was unlucky. The no-AI arm already delivered 61.5% before the pilot against 66.9%, so against each arm’s own before-period the gap is 5.2 on easy quarters and 4.1 on hard.

On the structure, with AI in both arms, the new structure delivered 0.8 points less on easy quarters and 8.9 less on hard ones, and the average and the median disagree, since its median delivery (71.4%) matched engineer-managers with AI while its average (61.7%) fell below 66.7%. It holds by team (0.2 down with AI, 5.8 in the new structure) and without the first pilot quarter (7.3 points less on hard quarters), though shuffled team labels reach that gap one time in six.

On hard quarters the new structure’s median wait was shorter (24.6 hours against 27.8, two blank waits left out) but its average longer (83.0 against 29.4), and on easy quarters its median was longer.

Coordination improved as predicted, and delivery still fell. Easy-quarter escalations were 36% lower with AI, ratings were higher under professional managers (0.78 against 0.69, 33 blank left out), and blocked hours fell from 16.2 to 10.9, only in the new structure.

And the new structure’s hard quarters split. Either way, nearly twice as many delivered under 30% as under engineer-managers with AI (23 against 12, then 18 against 10), and every wait over 100 hours landed there. Those waits come from 9 of 40 teams, against 1 of 40 under engineer-managers with AI. On hard quarters they grew (2, 3, 4, 5), so it is not a first-quarter effect (across all quarters, 4, 4, 4, 5).

4. Against the model

The Brief named three ways the model would be wrong, and two hold, at either summary of the wait. The difference with AI is nearly as large on hard quarters as easy, so the first holds. The new structure’s median wait is shorter on hard quarters only, and its delivery is 8.9 points lower, so at the median the third falsifier holds, and at the average the second.

But the median hides the hard quarters with a wait over 100 hours, so the queue may limit delivery.

5. What this does not establish

Three explanations fit a hard-quarter shortfall, and the file can test two. If leads were overloaded, I would expect backlogs, but escalations were open at quarter’s close in 1% of the new structure’s team-quarters against 34% to 42% elsewhere, so backlogs don’t fit, though the long waits do, and the drop may be a tracker change.

If AI misled teams on hard work, every AI arm would suffer there, but engineer-managers with AI beat those without (55.3% against 45.8%).

My Data & Methods concern, misjudged difficulty, shrinks hard–easy differences, so the shortfall is, if anything, understated. Waits and delivery share a quarter, so a failing quarter can cause long waits, and splitting on them selects quarters after the lot.

The decision needs a model that explains, because the average hides a split, and only what splits it says where it works.

What would settle it is a better diagram, not more of the same data. The shortfall sits in the new structure on hard work, within it in quarters whose waits explode, and AI alone does not show it. Every escalation there passes between the lead and the manager, and our diagram has no box for that. Module 3 draws it, and that box is where to look first, measured from the first month.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) for the comparisons and charts. It judged the wait prediction contradicted from the all-quarter average, so I added the before-periods and the median and kept the long waits.

Work it yourself: the Results prompts version 2

These are the prompts used to write the Results draft above, in order, in the same chat as the Data & Methods prompts (or a new one with fernhill_v2.csv uploaded again, and fernhill_ai_usage.csv before P16). Think about the question before you open “What we found.” Gemini’s charts and wording will differ from ours, but the numbers should match. If a number doesn’t, that’s a check worth running.

A rerun on Gemini 4. We ran every prompt again on November 16 with Gemini’s newer model (the shared chat is https://gemini.google.com/share/d/1L3ukbrI0Up9kUio2GSfEAZk94D-X2nU0?usp=sharing). Every number came out as it does here, and the notes that begin “In a rerun” say what was different. Part way through, Gemini said the file was no longer attached. If yours does, attach it again and repeat the prompt.

This model is bigger than version 1’s. Three arms, easy and hard quarters, a before-period for each arm, a mechanism (the wait) and three rival explanations make a dozen analyses, and the draft has two pages and two charts. So the prompts do two jobs. They ask Gemini for every number the draft needs, and they tell it exactly what each chart must show, because a chart you don’t specify is a chart you will redo. Two things recur in the chart prompts. Say what one dot or one bar is, and say which column defines the groups (hard_plan, rated at planning, never hard_close, rated after the outcome). Then decide what to leave out. Some of what the prompts find, such as the easy-quarter escalations in P17, the draft leaves out for room.

See exactly how we ran it Gemini's answers to these prompts, step by step (the shared chat, which opens when you sign in with your Willamette account).

P7

What is compared with what?

Count the team-quarters and the distinct teams in each arm, separately for the periods before and during the pilot. Then tell me whether manager_type and ai_access are the same for every team in each arm during the pilot, and which rows have a value for hard_plan.

The lot assigned teams, not team-quarters. How many independent units does each arm really have?

What we found
Before the pilot During the pilot Teams
EM_noAI (engineer-manager, no AI) 320 160 40
EM_AI (engineer-manager, AI) 320 160 40
ML_AI (manager + lead, AI) 320 160 40

During the pilot each arm is exactly one manager type and one AI setting, so an arm comparison changes one thing at a time, which version 1’s file could not do. Every team is an engineer-manager without AI before July 2025. hard_plan is blank for all 960 team-quarters before the pilot and filled for all 480 during it (210 hard, 270 not). Each arm has 40 teams, so arm comparisons rest on 40 teams, not on 480 team-quarters. Keep that in mind whenever Gemini reports a very small difference as certain.

P8

Did the lot balance the arms?

For each arm, give the average delivered_share over the eight quarters before the pilot, with the number of team-quarters.

If teams were assigned by lot, how different would you expect the arms to be before anything changed?

What we found
Before the pilot Team-quarters
EM_noAI 61.5% 320
EM_AI 66.9% 320
ML_AI 67.4% 320

The no-AI arm started 5 to 6 points behind. With 40 teams an arm, a lot can be unlucky by chance. It is not a flaw in the pilot, but it means a raw gap between arms mixes what AI did with where each arm began. That is why every comparison from here also sets each arm against its own before-period.

P9

The first chart

Make one dot plot. Put the three arms on the y axis (EM_noAI, EM_AI, ML_AI) and the average delivered_share on the x axis, from 40% to 80%. Interpretation version 2

1. My causal claim

Giving AI to teams run by engineer-managers raised their delivery. With each team set against its own eight quarters before the pilot, the lot puts the gain at 4.3 points (a 90% range of about 0 to 9), 4.2 on easy quarters and 3.1 on hard ones. The new structure, a professional manager and a technical lead with AI, delivered less than engineer-managers with AI, 5.6 points less over the year (about −12 to 1), 6.9 less on hard quarters (about −15 to 1) and no different on easy ones (0.1, about −6 to 6), and its teams spread much further apart. The person holding technical judgment left far more often in the new structure, a lead in 18 of 160 team-quarters against the most senior engineer in 5 of 160 under engineer-managers with AI. Why the new structure falls short on hard work, this file can’t say.

2. My causal diagram

The lot set who got which structure and AI, so no back door reaches the arm comparisons. What the file can’t show is the step the shortfall runs through. On hard quarters the new structure’s median wait for an escalation was shorter (24.6 hours against 27.8), but its average was far longer (83.0 against 29.4), because 7 of the 35 new-structure teams with a hard quarter had a wait over 100 hours, against 1 of 35 under engineer-managers with AI. The rival I took most seriously is that the leads were simply overloaded. If so, escalations would pile up unanswered, but they were open at quarter’s close in 1% of the new structure’s team-quarters, against 34% to 42% elsewhere. So the queue empties, slowly for some teams. Every escalation in the new structure passes between a manager and a lead, and my diagram has no box for that handoff, so I’ve drawn it dashed. It is my best guess at the missing step, and nothing in this file measures it.

3. The rung my evidence reaches

The arm comparisons reach doing, the second rung. The lot is an experiment, and setting each team against its own before-period makes it a comparison of changes inside one. That matters here, because the lot left AI’s two arms apart before the pilot (61.5% against 66.9%). Raw, AI’s gain is about twice what I report. With 40 teams a side the ranges are wide. AI’s direction is fairly sure and its size is not. The structure’s ranges reach just above zero, so a small benefit isn’t ruled out, though most of the range is a loss. The long waits reach seeing, the first rung. Waits and delivery share a quarter, so a failing quarter can cause a long wait, and picking quarters by their wait selects them after the lot. The departures reach doing, by lot. Shuffling the arm labels across the 80 teams reaches a gap that large about one time in 800, though a lead who once managed and a senior engineer who never did are different roles.

What I tried. The Results draft compared the arms raw, by difficulty, by team, without the first pilot quarter, at the median and the average, and through the waits, backlogs, escalations, ratings and blocked hours. This section adds the six before-period comparisons and the departures. I report the before-period version of every arm comparison, whichever way it moved the number.

4. What it would take to know more

The next step is to measure the handoff, not to run the same trial longer. With the new structure’s teams spreading by 22.5 points, seeing a 5-point difference with fair confidence would take about 320 teams a side, far more than Fernhill has. A better diagram is cheaper than more teams. If the shortfall runs through the working relationship between manager and lead, a short monthly survey of every pair from the first month, and a count of how often the manager overrides the lead’s estimates, would show it early and pair by pair. Is it worth it? A pulse survey costs a few minutes a month for each pair. Being wrong about the structure costs, on this evidence, about 6 points of delivery across 120 teams, and leads leaving. So measuring the handoff is worth it before any decision to expand the new structure.

5. My forecast for the decision

I recommend giving AI to every engineer-manager’s team now, and not rolling out the new structure until the handoff has been measured.

If Fernhill gives AI to all its engineer-managers’ teams, I expect delivery between about 0 and 9 points higher over the next year than without it, most likely about 4, or up to about 870 more of the roughly 9,700 milestones a year’s teams commit (about 420 most likely). This assumes the gain travels from the 40 pilot teams to the other 80, the tools stay as they are, and the 2025 customer migration was a one-off shared by every team.

If instead Fernhill moved all 120 teams to the new structure, I expect delivery between about 12 points lower and 1 point higher than engineer-managers with AI, most likely about 6 lower (about 1,160 fewer to 100 more milestones a year), with more teams far from the average and more leads leaving. This assumes the professional managers hired for 120 teams are as good as the 40 hired for the pilot, enough leads stay, and about 44% of quarters stay hard. A thinner pool of managers at scale would move this range down.

For whom or when might it not hold? The loss is on hard work, where the range runs from about −15 to 1, and on easy work the new structure did no worse. Teams with mostly easy work are where it might hold its own, and teams with mostly hard work, and long escalation queues, are where it is most likely to fail.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) for every comparison in this section, with the prompts below (P23 to P27), and checked its numbers against the course’s script. Every number matched. It resampled whole teams as asked, and it counted the long waits against the 35 teams in each arm that had a hard quarter, not all 40, which I had missed, so I use its count. It did not say that a failing quarter can cause a long wait, or that the departures compare two different roles, so I added both.

Does the person holding technical judgment leave more often?

In the pilot quarters of EM_AI and ML_AI, count the team-quarters with lead_departed = yes in each arm, out of 160. Then take each of the 80 teams' share of quarters with a departure, shuffle the arm labels among the 80 teams 20,000 times, and tell me how often the shuffled ML_AI minus EM_AI gap is at least as large as the real one.

Under engineer-managers, lead_departed records the most senior engineer leaving. Is that the same role as a lead?

What we found
Pilot team-quarters Departures Of
ML_AI (the lead left) 18 160
EM_AI (the most senior engineer left) 5 160

Shuffling the labels reaches a gap this large about one time in 800. The roles differ, so read it as “the person holding technical judgment left far more often”, by lot.

In our run Gemini gave 18 and 5 of 160, noticed that no team lost more than one, and reached the gap in 31 of 20,000 shuffles (0.16%), adding the exact figure (0.13%, about one in 780) unasked. Your own shuffle will land near these. It did not raise the THINK question, that the two arms record different roles.

P25

Where is the shortfall?

For the pilot quarters rated hard at planning, give the median and the average esc_wait_hrs in ML_AI and in EM_AI, and the number of teams in each arm with at least one hard quarter whose esc_wait_hrs is over 100.

If the median wait is shorter in the new structure, why might its delivery on hard work still be lower?

What we found
Hard pilot quarters Median wait, hours Average wait, hours Teams with a wait over 100 hours
ML_AI 24.6 83.0 7 of 35
EM_AI 27.8 29.4 1 of 35

The typical wait is shorter, but a few teams’ waits explode. That points to something that goes wrong in some new-structure teams and not others, which the file has no column for. It is the first rung, since a failing quarter can also cause a long wait.

In our run Gemini gave every figure and listed each long wait by team. It counted the teams against the 35 in each arm that had a hard pilot quarter, not all 40, which is the right denominator, so we changed ours to match. It also noted one missing wait in each arm, left out of the median and average. It did not say that a long wait can follow a failing quarter rather than cause it.

P26

What would it take to know more?

In ML_AI, take each team's change in delivered_share (pilot minus its own pre average, in percentage points) and give its standard deviation. Using the rule of thumb that a comparison of two groups of n teams each sees a gap of d points with about 80% power when n is 2 × (2.8 × sd / d) squared, how many teams a side would a lot need to see a 5-point difference?

Is a longer or larger trial the cheapest way to learn why the new structure falls short on hard work?

What we found

The standard deviation is 22.5 points, so about 320 teams a side (318) for a 5-point difference, far more than Fernhill has. Measuring the step the shortfall runs through is cheaper than counting more teams.

In our run Gemini gave 22.48 and 318 a side, nearly eight times the pilot’s 40, and a second answer (310) from a population standard deviation. It did not weigh a larger trial against measuring the handoff, which the THINK question leaves to you.

P27

The forecast in milestones

Sum milestones_committed over the 480 pilot team-quarters. Then turn the AI comparison (4.3 points, about 0 to 9) and the structure comparison (−5.6 points, about −12 to 1) into milestones a year at that scale, and give the share of pilot quarters rated hard at planning.

A decision-maker counts milestones, not percentage points. Which assumptions does turning one into the other add?

What we found

The pilot year committed 9,701 milestones. AI’s 4.3 points is about 420 more delivered on time a year (0 to about 870), and the structure’s −5.6 is about 540 fewer (about 1,160 fewer to 100 more). Of the pilot quarters, 43.8% were rated hard at planning. Turning points into milestones assumes the firm keeps committing about as many, and that next year’s mix of hard work looks like this one’s.

In our run Gemini gave 9,701 and 43.75%, and turned both the rounded and the unrounded comparisons into milestones (about 417 and 412 for AI, about 543 and 540 for the structure), with each arm’s commitments and share of hard quarters unasked. It did not state the assumptions, which belong in your forecast.

Earlier: version 1, the enthusiast's model

This is a complete project through its Interpretation, with careful, honest work on a model that turned out to be incomplete, and the reason the next version exists. It stays here because we learn from mistakes too.

Show version 1

Download fernhill_v1.csv

What version 2 taught us version 3

Version 2 asked two questions by lot, what AI alone adds and what the new structure adds, and its Results draft answered the first and found something odd in the second. This entry records what the draft found, what we noticed but set aside, what we decided to do about it and why, and what changed in the project as a result. When a model changes, everything built on it changes too, so version 3 redoes the Project Brief, the Data & Methods draft and the Results draft from the start.

What version 2 found

  • AI alone added 10.7 points on easy quarters and 9.5 on hard ones, raw, and 5.2 and 4.1 against each arm’s own before-period. The no-AI arm had been behind before the pilot (61.5% against about 67%), so the lot was unlucky, and the before-period caught it.
  • The new structure delivered less on hard quarters, not more. The new structure delivered 0.8 points less on easy quarters and 8.9 less on hard ones, the opposite of the Brief’s prediction of about 5 more. Leaving out the first pilot quarter, in case of a honeymoon or learning effect, changed nothing important (7.3 points less on hard quarters).
  • The median hid something. The new structure’s median wait on hard quarters was shorter (24.6 hours against 27.8), as the model said, but its average was nearly three times longer (83.0 against 29.4), because 14 of its 73 hard quarters waited over 100 hours, against 1 of 69. Every one of those long waits landed in quarters that delivered under 30%. Without them, the new structure’s hard quarters delivered as engineer-managers with AI did.
  • Backlogs were almost absent in the new structure (1% of team-quarters, against 34% to 42% under engineer-managers), so the long waits were not simple overload.

So the new structure fails on hard work, in the quarters where a wait explodes, and the typical wait is shorter. An average and a median are not two ways of saying the same thing.

Why we didn’t conclude “it failed”

Three explanations fit the averages, and version 2 could test only two of them.

  1. Leads overloaded. Backlogs don’t fit it, though the long waits do.
  2. AI misleading teams on hard work. If it were, every arm with AI would suffer there, but engineer-managers with AI delivered 55.3% on hard quarters against 45.8% without.
  3. Some manager and lead pairs work, and others don’t. Version 2 had no way to see a pair, so it could not test this one.

What is left is something specific to the new structure, worst on hard work, that also seems to drive leads out.

Noticed, not pursued (yet)

  • Lead departures: 11.2% of new-structure teams a quarter, against 3% to 4% under engineer-managers, and all 18 who left had been the team’s manager before the lead role. Version 1 had seen the same rise and let it go.
  • AI’s gain on hard quarters came out nearly as large as on easy ones (4.1 against 5.2). It could be noise or a gap in the model, and version 3 carries it as an open question, not a new mechanism.
  • IT’s usage logs, which version 2 used only to check that the no-AI arm stayed off licensed tools, also show how much each licensed team really used AI. Version 3 looks at that.

What we decided, and why

We drew how an escalated unknown actually gets resolved in the new structure. The lead judges the technical path, the manager sets priorities, and the two must agree. Every escalation crosses the relationship between the manager and the lead. That box was in no earlier diagram, so no earlier version could have a column for it. (See “Three diagrams, one firm”.)

Decision Why
Model the relationship: escalations cross it, it evolves from the pair’s fit, the lead’s lost status and the manager’s technical grasp, results and HR reshape it, and weak relationships drive departures The new structure fails on hard work, splits, and loses leads, and neither the queue nor AI explains it
Measure it with a monthly pulse from month one, in every arm (under engineer-managers, the manager and the most senior engineer) A relationship forms at the start. Measured later, it would show only the pairs that survived, and relationships already shaped by results. Every arm, so the structures can be compared
Add an override count from the planning tool’s audit log A behavior is harder to game than an answer, and a score that decides something will be gamed
Register pairs, with a pair ID The relationship belongs to the pair, and pairs change when a lead leaves
Let HR act on the scores in half the new-structure teams, chosen by a second lot If HR acts on every low score, low scores rise on their own and HR takes the credit. The lot gives a fair comparison
Add backlog carry-over and firefighting to the queue The backlog column showed engineer-managers’ queues carrying over for quarters
Add the manager’s technical grasp and the 2025 skill premium Crossing the relationship takes shared knowledge, and managers hired on people skill in 2025 tend to be weaker technically
Recast the hard-quarter prediction Version 2 already showed the new structure doing worse on hard quarters, so version 3 predicts where that comes from, weak pairs, instead of predicting it again
Carry AI over unchanged The engineer-manager arms are the same teams, so version 2’s AI result stands and can’t be repeated as new evidence

A note on the data. Fernhill is a simulation, so we can replay the same year at the same firm (the same 120 teams, the same people, the same luck) with the design version 2’s results call for. A real firm gets one try, which is why the model has to come before the data.

What changed in the Project Brief

Element Version 2 Version 3
What Fernhill does A pilot by lot, three arms of 40 The same, plus People Operations measures the relationship from month one
The model Two jobs, split between a manager and a lead, with unknowns queuing at whoever holds technical judgment Adds a third job, keeping the two roles working together, and seven numbered mechanisms, with the relationship in the middle
In short AI helps most on easy work, and the new structure helps most on hard work The relationship decides whether the new structure works, above all on hard work
Must be true People skill really higher, and leads accept the role The score tracks the working relationship, not politeness, and enough leads exist to make re-pairing possible
Unmeasured The judgment holder’s capacity, seen only through waits The pair’s fit, and capacity, seen only through the relationship and the waits
The question Two comparisons by lot Adds HR’s response, HR acting against scores sealed
The prediction AI helps on easy work, ratings are higher, and the structure helps hard quarters AI as before. The score predicts delivery more in the new structure and on hard work. Hard quarters split by the relationship. Departures follow weak pairs. HR helps modestly
The model is wrong if AI helps as much on hard work, waits aren’t shorter, or shorter waits don’t help The score adds nothing beyond escalation load, weak and strong pairs deliver alike, or HR raises scores but not delivery or retention
The data sketch Arm, size, difficulty at planning, escalations, waits Adds HR’s lot, technical score, difficulty at close, open escalations, the pulse and overrides, coaching, re-pairing, departures
The anchor Organizations and operations Adds technical competence and status, firefighting, integration and relational coordination
The method A randomized pilot Draw the model before the data

What changed in the Data & Methods draft

Section Version 2 Version 3
Unit A team-quarter, 40 teams to an arm A team-quarter with a pair ID, 40 teams to an arm and 20 a side in HR’s lot. A second file, one row per pair per month, joins on pair ID and quarter together
Variables Arm, before or after, escalations, waits, difficulty, delivery Arm, the relationship score, difficulty, waits, lead departures, delivery
Data source Four systems and a usage log, simulated from a model the draft doesn’t see Adds the pulse and the audit log, and the draft states the simulation’s assumptions
Quality concern Difficulty at planning The score, which people can answer politely and HR can teach pairs to raise, checked against overrides
First description Delivery, waits, difficulty Delivery, the score and its monthly path, waits

What changed in the Results draft

Section Version 2 Version 3
Question What the arms deliver Whether the relationship decides it, and whether HR’s tending matters
Charts Delivery by arm, and where each arm’s hard quarters end up Hard quarters by arm and by the score, and HR’s teams against sealed ones
Against the model Two of three ways to be wrong hold None of the first two holds, and the third can’t be judged in a year
What it can’t say Why a few waits explode Whether the relationship causes delivery, since nobody assigned it, and what HR’s response did, since 20 teams a side is too few to tell from chance

Lines that didn’t change are word for word the same where they can be, so what changed is exactly what the new model required.
